109	## 4. The bound: P-42 holds, on these grounds
110	
111	**L1.** (a) POPL 2019, the type group's last published word, Steele and Ryu among the authors: "By default, each type parameter has an upper bound Any" (`ParkPOPL2019.txt:418-419`). (b) The WD's `Object` sentence (`trait-parameters.tex:49-50`) is absent from the 2008 release (page 67), enters the repository in two bulk imports of 2009-11, the first in a chapter headed "Not Yet Implemented Features"; its composer is not recoverable. The same WD section says "Type parameters are instantiated with types such as trait types, tuple types, and arrow types" (`:53-54`), and the WD puts tuples, arrows and `()` outside `Object` (`types-vals-vars.tex:136`, `:215-216`); so under the WD's own `Object` default no unbounded parameter could take what the WD says parameters take. (c) The library, the team's statement of the language's library, declares its element parameters unbounded and instantiates them at tuples (`Generator[\E\]`, `zip`'s `(E,F)`); only six functions write `extends Any`. (d) The 2012 Types chapter states no default and makes `Any` the top with `Object` excluding `Void` and every tuple type (`types.tick:232-238`); Welterweight and the 2011 paper have `Any` as the top. (e) The team's own 2008 commit left the bound "(either Object or Any)" open. Naden's August 2012 theory calls `Object` "the distinguished top type" in a calculus with no tuples or arrows, where the two names coincide; it is not a vote for `Object` over tuples.
112	
113	**L2, the archaeology's finding and how to read it.** Steele implemented the WD's sentence on 2012-05-28 ("amazingly, this was not yet implemented"), inserting `extends Any` into the compiled libraries and nine tests wherever they instantiated at `()`, a tuple, an arrow or `Any`; commented it out on 05-29 "so that interpreter tests will pass"; and on 05-30 made it a setting, on in `useCompilerLibraries`, off in `useInterpreterLibraries`. The brief's phrase "Steele's 2012 code chose `Object` as the language's rule" reads too much into it. His message says he was implementing a sentence already written, not deciding one; when the sentence broke walk's tests he did not change walk or the library, he confined the sentence to the compiled path; and he had to write `Any` by hand everywhere the compiled world needed tuples. No team text says the code generator, class loader or RTTI needs `Object` (archaeology §2.6, §5). The code reads the other way: Naden's dispatcher ignores a written `Any` bound as "meaningless" and checks any other (`OverloadSet.java:1516-1517`); `FnNameInfo.boundsFor` names an empty clause `Object` only in a generic method's name, which declaration and call compute alike. The team's texts after 2012-05-30 (Types, 05-31; Naden, 08-31; POPL 2019) do not carry `Object` as the default. So the setting is the compiled path's departure from the language's rule, L2, and ends by one line.

170	## 9. For Pavol
171	
172	**What you asked.** On 26 October you wrote that you doubted whether the decisions the revival rests on were good and well informed, or a mistake. You named the bound as a possible linchpin, and you asked that the three layers be kept apart: what the Fortress language says; how the team built it on the Java virtual machine; and how Fortress meets Java.
173	
174	**The verdict, first.**
175	
176	- None of the nine foundational decisions was a mistake. All nine hold.
177	- Three of them were taken on information that was incomplete or partly wrong. In every case, the missing or corrected fact makes your decision stronger or leaves it as it is. None weakens it.
178	- The layers were mixed in the reasons written under your decisions, not in the decisions. Four entries give a reason from the wrong layer, or call a 2009 piece of code "later" than a 2011 paper. The rewrites fix the reasons. No decision turns.
179	
180	**The bound, in plain words.** A type parameter is a placeholder for a type, like the `T` in `List[\T\]`. Its bound is the largest type the placeholder may stand for. `Any` is the type of every value. `Object` is the type of every value except tuples (pairs such as `(3, 4)`), functions, and the empty value `()`. You decided that a placeholder with no written bound means `Any`.
181	
182	- The language, layer one, says `Any`. The team's last paper, from 2019, with Steele and Ryu among its authors, says in so many words that the default bound is `Any`. The team's library, which is their statement of the language's library, writes its placeholders without a bound and fills them with tuples. The 2011 draft's sentence saying `Object` is not in the 2008 text, appears in 2009 in a list of "Not Yet Implemented Features", and sits beside a sentence in the same section saying placeholders take tuple types, which `Object` would forbid.
183	- The team's build on the virtual machine, layer two, does not need `Object`. In May 2012 Steele implemented the draft's sentence on the compiled path, saying it was "amazingly" not yet implemented. The next day it broke the interpreter's tests. He did not change the interpreter or the library. He made the sentence a setting that is on for the compiled path and off for the interpreter, and he wrote `Any` by hand in every compiled library and test that needed tuples. That is enforcing a sentence on one path, not choosing the language's rule. No team text says the compiled path needs `Object`. A probe this week turned the setting off: tuples and functions as type arguments compile and run exactly as they do today when `Any` is written. With the setting on, as the compile command has it today, a call `id((3, 4))` compiles and silently runs `id(3)`.
184	- Java, layer three, maps its own `Object` type to Fortress `Any`, not to Fortress `Object`. Nothing in the record ever used Java as a reason for the bound.
185	- What you were told on 29 September had two errors: that "nothing in the code changes" (one line in `Shell.java` does), and that the 2012 Types chapter puts functions outside `Object` (it puts them inside; tuples stay outside). No selection at run time; the model names the `RR64` factory, and `vector[\RR64,s\]` stays boxed. An element read through the generic trait's `get` still returns a box unless decision B unboxes by static type (my reading).
5. **A5, a special type,** the compiled world's own precedent: an `RR64Vector` lowered to its Java class by the code generator's table, as `ZZ32Vector` is (FACTS line 160). A type the specification does not have; the model names it.

**What each costs.** A1: the store class and object, the bodies of the generic factories (`vector`, `matrix`, `array1` to `array3` and their value and function forms), a cast per array made; measured to check and run on both paths. A2: the same store, one plain factory per native element type, and walk's family check. A3: the store and one factory per element type; a model line wherever a factory is named. ## Tenet 7. Unboxed doubles and `double[]` arrays (P-17, P-84), on the compiled path's template classes

### (a) The entries

POS.md:16:

> - P-17 **Unboxed doubles and arrays of unboxed doubles are required: without them the revival misses its point.** Why: a language meant for high performance cannot box its numbers. Today the code generator boxes every number: an `RR64` value is an object of the class `FRR64`. In Java models of microGPT's three array kernels, the dot product, the matrix product and the row lift, boxing is the main cost (F-11 holds the measurement). How arrays store doubles, as `double[]`, is P-84's decision.

POS.md:92:

> - P-84 **An `RR64` array is stored as a Java `double[]`, unboxed, and arrays keep the team's `nat` sizes in their types.** Why: a high-performance language cannot box its array elements, and the sizes are central to the team's design. So the storage and the sizes are one design: the sizes stay in the array types as `nat` static parameters, as the library's `Vector` and `Matrix` declare them, and the compiled checker checks them. The sizes do not wait while a first version of the store carries them only as run-time fields; that layered plan was rejected. Both halves follow the library's own patterns (P-27, the library's own practice is the standard). The compiled checker checks `nat` static parameters (F-67). The compiled path's `double[]` store waits with the other array decisions until after the switch-over; among them is decision A, how an `RR64` array made through the library's generic array traits gets that store (P-85).

- P-26 **Where the team's later word on the language conflicts with the specification's early text, the later word wins; each ground is weighed in its own layer, and "later" is a date.** The team's word has three layers. The language: the Working Draft of February 2011, whose text the team last edited in 2010-12, and `Specification/`, the revival's revision of it (P-7); the 2012 Types chapter; the type group's papers; and the team's library, the interpreter's, as their statement of the language's library. A team text of the language that argues from Java, as the 2011 paper does, still counts in the language. The team's implementation on the JVM: the compiled checker, the code generator, the class loader, the run time, the compiler's prelude and walk. Java interoperability: how Fortress types and natives meet Java's. A ground in one layer may confirm, but does not by itself decide, a question in another, and a JVM or checker limit never overrides what the language's texts say. Where those texts give no answer, the curator decides by the goal (P-8), and a ground in the implementation may weigh there (P-77). In the language, later texts that agree with each other rank above earlier ones, by year: the Working Draft (text of 2010), the type group's paper (2011, `Papers/Types/`), the Types chapter and Karl Naden's write-up "The Return Type Rule and Generics" (both 2012, the write-up at `Papers/Types/journal/justificationOfRTR.tex`), and the POPL 2019 paper, the last (F-166). Where the specification conflicts with them, it is revised to follow them (P-95 records each change with its reason). The team's code in the implementation counts as their word on the language only where they wrote the rule on purpose: in a text, a commit message, a code comment, or a checker rule enforced as the language's. A stub by the team's own words, such as a line they called "bogus" or a "temporary hack", does not count, and neither does a workaround of a JVM or checker gap. Before you call a commit later, date it against the texts: a 2009 change to the compiler's prelude is earlier than the 2011 paper. Where two later sources conflict, this rule gives no order: the curator decides by the goal (P-8), and the record says that the goal decided it. Two things are called specialisation. A specialised overload is a version of a generic function for one instantiation, such as `tail(x: List[ZZ])` beside `tail[X](x: List[X])`, which dispatch chooses at run time; it belongs to the language. Stamping is the class loader's making of one class for each instantiation; it belongs to the implementation. Why: the early text was a wish, written early and in a vacuum; the type group learned what is feasible by building it, with performance as the goal and specialised overloads a must; the revival knows less than they did and does not second-guess them. That reason is evidence about the implementation. The ground in the language: the Working Draft contradicts itself, since its types chapter makes the number types mutually exclusive and its library chapters make ℤ a subtype of ℚ, and the later texts agree with each other on the exclusion rule, the overloading rules and the default bound.

## 3. Row 816 and P-158 (10-25 19:06 to 10-26 04:28)

**The argument, in the order he asked for it (19:35:13):**

1. *The two paths call a method differently.* Walk finds a method on the object by name at the call; the trait need not declare it. The compiled path calls through the trait's Java interface; if the trait does not declare the method, the call dies with `NoSuchMethodError`.
2. *The team's two libraries each followed their path.* The compiler's prelude: the api writes `abstract loop(body: ZZ32->()): ()` in `GeneratorZZ32`; the component restates `loop(body: ZZ32->()): ()` with no body; the objects give the body (`Library/CompilerLibrary.fsi:112-120`, `.fss:301-312`). Chase's 2012 export check (`5a68404fd`) enforced it: a component trait with fewer members than its api trait is refused. The interpreter's library, written for walk and never compiled by the team, sometimes leaves an api's `abstract` member out of the component's trait (`String`'s `split`), and walk does not care.
3. *What the revival changed.* When the checker read the interpreter's library, Chase's check refused 12 such members. Two ways: (a) add the 12 declarations to the components, the compiled library's way; (b) weaken the check. Climb batch 21b's rung E took (b) (`031c38bbc`), from a misreading of `apis.tex` ("includes definitions for all declarations other than … abstract" read as "needs no member", where it says "needs no body"). The chain: an Opus ways worker of 10-20 (`reviews/array-sites-ways.md`, "4i", "Decision: none, since it is the text's own rule"); the export probe of 10-23 built it; batch 21's planner made it fork 20 with the default "the team's own text"; its Fable review and I passed it as not consequential; rung E built it; its skeptic found the `NoSuchMethodError` after the build; the 21b review kept it as "it cannot happen yet"; batch 22 carried it as question 1 and I launched batch 22 at about 02:01 on 10-24 without sending him the question. No document before the change mentions `NoSuchMethodError`. Root cause: one sentence misread; nobody read the code it changed (Chase's deliberate count) or asked what a compiled call does; the change cleared errors, which was the batch's goal.
4. *The fix (his option 2).* Restore Chase's count; add 12 bodyless declarations to five component traits (`String` 7: `depth`, `isBalanced`, `verify`, `rangeContains`, `balanced`, `splitWithOffsets`, `split`; `Range`'s `isEmpty`; `ReadableArray`'s `opr[_:TrivialOpenRange]`; `ActualReduction`'s `empty` and `join`; `AnyMaybe`'s `holds`). No body, not an empty body: an empty body makes the method concrete, and then no object must define it.

**His decision:** option 2 (19:06:08 on 10-25); his reason (04:28:41 on 10-26): "by the standing position that later team's work supersedes earlier one, we take the compiled path's way over the walk library's. That's why 21b should have chosen (a), not weaken the check — we must reverse this." 9:### The words this record uses
12:- A **native binding** is a library body `builtinPrimitive("…")`, a declaration whose code is Java. Today every string names a **glue class**, Java over walk's own values, which the compiled path cannot call (F-32). A **helper** is a static Java method over plain Java values in `nativeHelpers/`, the compiled path's kind. By your decision P-58, each string comes to name a helper: walk loads it beside its glue classes, and the compiled path rewrites the body at the parse into a call of it.
13:- To **move** a binding is to change its string from a glue class to a helper. A **family** is a set of bindings moved together, as `ZZ32`'s.
17:### Where the natives stand
19:- **449 live bindings on the base, sorted into F-32's classes** by the natives probe's own scripts: 154 the prelude binds at the same owner and signature (A), 59 with a helper that nothing binds (B), 158 that need a new helper (C), 36 methods of the I/O objects (D1) and 42 with no compiled analogue (D2) (section 4).
